text: Few passages in the Hebrew Bible have had a stranger reception than the brief notice of the *bnei elohim* ("sons of God") in Genesis 6. The Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish work preserved most fully in Ethiopic versions and still read as scripture by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, built an elaborate tradition on these verses. In its account the sons of God are fallen angels, the Watchers, who came down to corrupt humanity in two ways: by forbidden teaching and by miscegenation. Two New Testament letters may presuppose this reading (Jude 6, 2 Peter 2:4). Augustine, in *City of God*, rejected the angelic interpretation and favored a Sethite one. On his reading the sons of God are the godly line of Seth, and the daughters of men belong to the line of Cain. Other readers have compared the passage with ancient Near Eastern traditions in which kings and other powerful men claimed descent from gods. The chapter also opens the flood narrative, and that narrative belongs to a broader Mesopotamian flood tradition. The fullest witnesses to that tradition are the *Atrahasis* epic and tablet XI of the *Epic of Gilgamesh* (the Utnapishtim narrative), and both carry close parallels to the biblical story. Even the vocabulary repays attention. The Hebrew word for the vessel Noah builds is *tevah* ("ark," "chest"). Outside the Noah story, Scripture uses *tevah* for only one other object: the basket in which the infant Moses is set adrift on the Nile.
